Woo Bum-kon (born January 4, 1957) is a South Korean classical pianist. He was born in Seoul, South Korea and began studying the piano at the age of five. He later studied at the Juilliard School in New York City with Adele Marcus and Sascha Gorodnitzki.

Woo Bum-kon made his debut at the age of 17 with the Berlin Philharmonic Orchestra under the direction of Herbert von Karajan in Berlin. Since then, he has performed with many of the world's leading orchestras, including the New York Philharmonic, London Symphony Orchestra, Berlin Philharmonic, and the Chicago Symphony Orchestra.

In addition to his concert career, Woo Bum-kon is also a dedicated teacher and has given masterclasses and lectures around the world. He is a professor at the Seoul National University of Arts and has been the Artistic Director of the Seoul International Spring Music Festival since 2002.

Woo Bum-kon is known for his interpretations of the works of Mozart, Chopin, and Beethoven, among others. He has also premiered several works by contemporary composers and has collaborated with artists such as Yo-Yo Ma and Emanuel Ax.

Woo Bum-kon has received numerous awards and honors for his contributions to music, including the Order of Cultural Merit from the government of South Korea and the Golden Bell Award for his contributions to Korean classical music. He is considered one of the greatest pianists of his generation and is highly regarded for his technical skill, expressive interpretations, and deep musical understanding.

Woo Bum-kon was a South Korean serial killer and rapist who committed his crimes in the 1980s. He is infamous for the brutal nature of his crimes, which included rape and murder, often with a high level of cruelty. Woo Bum-kon's killing spree took place between 1986 and 1991, in the cities of Asan, Cheonan, and other areas near the city of Seoul.

His modus operandi included attacking random women, mostly elderly or in vulnerable situations, and committing heinous acts against them. Woo Bum-kon would often torture and mutilate his victims, and he was known for leaving them in visible places to terrorize the public.

He was finally arrested in 1991, and during his trial, the gruesome details of his crimes shocked the nation. Woo Bum-kon confessed to 26 murders, though the actual number might be higher, as some victims' bodies were never found.

In South Korea, the case of Woo Bum-kon became a major societal issue, sparking discussions on mental health, societal safety, and the effectiveness of the justice system in handling such heinous crimes.

Woo Bum-kon was sentenced to death and executed in 1997, but the legacy of his atrocities continues to impact Korean society and the criminal justice system. His case also shed light on the need for better psychological evaluation and support for those who may commit such violent crimes.

Due to the horrific nature of his crimes, discussions and media around Woo Bum-kon are typically approached with sensitivity and a focus on the lessons learned from his case regarding public safety and the legal system's role in preventing and responding to such acts of violence.

Woo Bum-kon was a South Korean policeman who perpetrated one of the deadliest mass murders in modern history. On April 26, 1982, Woo Bum-kon went on a shooting spree in the villages of Uiryeong and Gamgong, South Korea, killing 56 people and injuring 35 others before taking his own life.

Woo Bum-kon was a 27-year-old police officer at the time, and his motives for the massacre are still not entirely clear. However, it is believed that he was motivated by a combination of factors, including a dispute with his girlfriend, a recent transfer to a rural police station, and a sense of frustration and disillusionment with his life.

On the day of the massacre, Woo Bum-kon began by shooting and killing several people in his girlfriend's family, including her parents and siblings. He then went on to shoot and kill numerous other people in the surrounding villages, including children, women, and the elderly.

The massacre was widely reported in the media, and it shocked the nation. It led to widespread outrage and calls for greater accountability and reform within the South Korean police force. Woo Bum-kon's actions were widely condemned, and he was posthumously stripped of his police honors.

The Woo Bum-kon massacre remains one of the deadliest mass murders in modern history, and it continues to be remembered as a tragic and senseless act of violence.
